newsitem.title: UK: Iran oil no trouble for Europe as eastern sales rise.
newsitem.headline: Iran oil no trouble for Europe as eastern sales rise.

text.p: Iran looks unlikely to trouble European oil markets with extra spot crude early this year despite the renewed competition from neighbour Iraq, oil traders and market analysts said on Thursday.

State-owned National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) has told European crude buyers that it has no spot cargo availabilities for the first quarter of the year because of higher term contract obligations and extra sales to the Far East, traders said.
"(NIOC) say they are sold out until the end of March," said a sour crude trader for a European refiner.
"They say they've got more under contract and they're taking more to the Far East...I'd think they're probably storing more too."
One Mediterranean refiner confirmed that it had upped the volume in its contract for Iranian crude but others reported no changes to contract volumes.
"They made a quite an effort (in 1996) to increase outlets in the Med, but it hasn't been the case this year," said one crude purchaser.
But market-watchers agreed that more Iranian crude was seen headed to markets East of Suez.

"There certainly has been a lot of new (refinery) capacity coming on the Far East in the last year and a lot of this appears to have been teamed up with Iranian crudes," said a Middle East trader for a European major.
Regional industry sources estimated that exports of Iranian crudes to the Far East rose by some 200,000 barrel per day (bpd) last year with most of the incremental sales headed for India and China.
In addition, Iranian domestic consumption has increased by 100-150,000 bpd over the last year, local sources said.
The resumption of Iraqi oil exports in December after a six-year break could have encouraged Iranian marketers to focus their efforts in markets outside Europe, traders said.
"I think they're quite happy to build up storage and try and sell more in the Far East," a trader said. "They don't want to put further pressure on Mediterranean sour diffs."
The return of Iraqi crude to world markets last month precipitated a sharp fall in values for Europe's benchmark sour crude Urals which lost nearly $1 a barrel off its value in the space of a week.
There have been no reported deals for Iranian grades in Europe for over a month, traders said.
Iranian Heavy was notionally pegged at Dated Brent -$1.80-$1.90 fob Sidi Kreir, with Iranian Light some 50 cents higher.
These levels are slightly higher than recent assessments, thanks to a modest recovery in values for Russian Urals.
Last year, spot sales accounted for around 100,000 bpd of the 500-600,000 bpd of Iranian exports through the Sumed pipeline to the Mediterranean terminal of Sidi Kreir, traders said.
